Task 1 - Inventory & Initial Scan
Course: Managing with Artificial Intelligence - Assignment T01, Task 1
How AI was used in this task
I used Claude (Anthropic) as a code-executing research assistant to automate metadata extraction: it ran pdfinfo "file.pdf" (reads embedded Title/Author/Subject/Keywords) and pdftotext -f 1 -l 2 "file.pdf" - | head -60 (extracts raw text of page 1-2 for the abstract, journal name and authors) on all 31 uploaded PDFs, and it checked uploaded filenames across both upload sessions for duplicates before compiling the inventory below.
Because this is a research-paper assignment, I also used Elicit, an AI tool purpose-built for reading and synthesizing academic literature, as a second, independent pass over the document archive. Elicit produced its own inventory, topic map and synthesis (referred to as 'the Elicit synthesis' throughout this and the following reports) which I used to cross-check Claude's clustering and to surface a few ideas Claude's pass had not produced - these additions are marked explicitly where they appear.
Section 4 below compares the two tools' extraction quality directly: Elicit worked from converted PDF text only and could not recover author/journal/date for many files, while the pdfinfo/pdftotext approach read this metadata straight from each PDF's embedded Info dictionary, giving a more bibliographically complete table here.
1. Duplicate check
Before extraction, the uploaded filenames were checked across both upload batches for duplicates. Five files had been uploaded twice (Optimal_scheduling_of_a_by-product_gas_supply_system..., Process_safety_4_0..., Research_on_modelling_and_optimization_of_hot_rolling_scheduling..., Simulation-Based_Multi-Criteria_Optimization_of..., sustainability-13-09277-v3.pdf). Each was kept and processed only once, giving a de-duplicated set of 31 unique documents.
2. Extraction method
Metadata was extracted automatically from each of the 31 PDFs using two command-line tools, run once per file:
pdfinfo "file.pdf"                          # reads embedded Title/Author/Subject/Keywords
pdftotext -f 1 -l 2 "file.pdf" - | head -60  # extracts raw text of page 1-2 (abstract, journal name, authors)
pdfinfo parses the PDF's Info dictionary, which is how fields such as Author or Keywords came directly out of the file without manual reading. pdftotext (poppler-utils) extracts the actual text layer of the first two pages so the abstract and journal header could be read to confirm the journal/year and write a one-line finding. Cluster assignment (used in Task 2) and the finding snippets below required manual reading and judgment, not automation.
3. Metadata inventory
4. Cross-check with an independent AI tool (Elicit)
Elicit was run separately over an archive it describes as containing 20 documents, a different (likely overlapping but not identical) scope than the 31 uploaded here, so document counts and numbering between the two tools are not directly comparable and are kept separate throughout this report.
Elicit's own Act I explicitly states that 'in many files, author, journal, and publication date were not present in the supplied converted excerpt', and that those fields were marked unavailable rather than inferred - because Elicit worked only from converted PDF text, not the PDFs' embedded metadata. The pdfinfo/pdftotext approach used here reads the PDF's Info dictionary directly, which recovered author, journal and year for effectively all 31 documents in the table above. This is a concrete methodological advantage of the command-line extraction approach for bibliographic completeness.
On the other hand, Elicit's independent reading of the same underlying literature converged strongly with the four questions this Task 1 scan already identified as central (metallurgical constraints, energy as a decision variable, disturbance handling, and governance of intelligence) - this agreement across two independently run AI tools is used as a validity check on the domain-boundary claim in Section 5 below, and is carried forward into Task 2's topic tree.
5. Boundaries of the knowledge domain
The 31 documents cluster around six main lines within 'AI for the steel industry': (A) Furnace & rolling scheduling optimization (classical OR/metaheuristics/matheuristics), (B) Reinforcement learning & LLM-assisted decision-making, (C) Digital twins & IoT-based production integration, (D) Energy & gas-flow management / process safety, (E) Explainable AI & human-AI trust, and (F) Multi-agent & market-based coordination. These clusters and the cross-references between them are developed in detail in Task 2, where they are also cross-checked against Elicit's independently generated five-layer topic map.

Task 2 - Topographical Mapping
Course: Managing with Artificial Intelligence - Assignment T01, Task 2
How AI was used in this task
I asked Claude to assign each of the 31 documents (extracted in Task 1) to one of several topic clusters based on their stated objectives and methods, and to identify which documents genuinely bridge two clusters rather than fitting one. Claude then wrote the Graphviz (dot language) code for both diagrams below and rendered it through the dot tool - I did not draw these by hand.
I also used Elicit, a research-paper-specialized AI tool, which independently produced its own five-layer topic map (mindmap) and cross-reference graph over its own document set. Section 4 below compares the two independently generated maps side by side; the strong structural agreement between them is used as a validity check on the clustering, and Elicit's naming of a central 'live scheduling' operating loop is carried forward into Task 4's blueprint.
1. Method
Building on the Task 1 metadata inventory, each of the 31 documents was assigned to a primary topic cluster based on its stated research objective and methodology (read from title, abstract and keywords). Six clusters emerged; documents whose methodology or application genuinely spans two clusters were flagged as cross-references. The hierarchical topic tree (Fig. 1) visualizes the taxonomy; the cross-reference network (Fig. 2) visualizes which documents structurally bridge two clusters - these bridging documents are the most valuable entry points for Task 3's deep dives, since they already combine two lines of thinking.
2. Hierarchical topic tree
Cluster sizes: A (17), B (6), C (5), D (2), E (5), F (2) - clusters overlap because several documents belong to more than one (e.g., [1] is both RL-based and Digital-Twin-based).
3. Cross-reference network
Colored edges mark the cross-cluster bridges that matter most for Task 3:
• Blue edges - Digital Twin <-> RL/Scheduling: [1, 4, 14, 29, 10, 5] form a connected chain. This is the strongest bridge in the whole set: digital twins are consistently used as the real-time data backbone that RL or metaheuristic schedulers act on.
• Purple edges - Process Safety/Trust <-> Explainable AI: [9, 31, 24, 26, 27] cluster tightly, showing that the 'can AI be trusted to decide' question recurs both as a safety argument ([9]) and as a technical XAI toolkit (24, 26, 27, 31).
• Orange edges - Energy optimization <-> Gas/Demand-response: [8, 9, 25, 28] connect gas-supply scheduling to electricity-market-aware DRL scheduling - both are 'energy as the optimization currency' papers.
• Red edge - Multi-agent coordination: [12, 18] are the only two papers using an agent/auction-based coordination paradigm rather than a central optimizer.
4. Cross-validation against an independent AI-generated map (Elicit)
Elicit organized its archive into a different but structurally similar five-layer mindmap: (1) Process truth - reheating physics, rolling metallurgy, flow integrity; (2) Energy system - furnace heat, utility coordination, sustainability metrics; (3) Decision engine - baseline optimization, scalable search, adaptive intelligence; (4) Digital thread - digital twins, IIoT data, simulation; (5) Assurance and organization - human-in-the-loop, XAI, safety governance. All five layers connect through a central 'Live scheduling' node running an Observe-Predict-Optimize-Explain-Approve-Execute-Learn loop.
The two independently run AI tools agree on the same five substantive ideas (physical constraints, energy objectives, a decision/optimization engine, a live-data layer, and human/XAI governance), which is a meaningful cross-validation of the taxonomy in Section 2. The one structural difference - my isolated Cluster F for multi-agent/market-based coordination - is a genuine judgment call rather than an error: [12, 18] use a fundamentally different coordination paradigm (auctions/decentralized agents) than every other document in the set (central optimizer or single policy), which is why I kept it separate.
Elicit's central 'live scheduling' loop (Observe - Predict - Optimize - Explain - Approve - Execute - Learn) also independently confirms this report's own network-graph finding that furnace & rolling scheduling (Cluster A) is the most-bridged, most-connected cluster in Section 3's graph - both analyses converge on scheduling as the organizing center of the whole document set. This operating loop is adopted explicitly in Task 4's blueprint.
5. Isolated sub-chains (no bridging document)
Three sub-chains have no cross-cluster bridge and therefore represent narrower, more self-contained streams of research:
• 2-3-13-21 - pure furnace-scheduling optimization (GA/GWO/online algorithms), all single-objective-adjacent and energy-focused.
• 7-17-15-20 - batch/heat-treatment scheduling under uncertainty (fuzzy logic, simulation-based multi-criteria).
• 16-23-22-19 - robustness-under-uncertainty scheduling (green scheduling, robust dynamic scheduling, proactive scheduling, robust HSM optimization) - a natural 'robustness' sub-topic for Task 3.
6. Implication for Task 3
The topology suggests candidate 'tension' pairs to dive into for Synthesis Divergence: (1) classical OR/metaheuristic scheduling vs. RL/DRL-based scheduling; (2) Digital Twins as passive monitoring vs. active real-time control substrate; (3) black-box optimization performance vs. Explainable AI transparency. Elicit's synthesis additionally surfaces a fourth tension - model fidelity vs. deployability - which is added to Task 3.

Task 3 - Synthesis Divergence
Course: Managing with Artificial Intelligence - Assignment T01, Task 3
How AI was used in this task
I directed Claude to re-examine the cross-reference network from Task 2 and identify the strongest recurring 'tensions' (points of genuine disagreement or trade-off) across the cluster, rather than simply summarizing each paper individually. Claude drafted the comparison tables below by extracting the relevant claims from each paper's findings (gathered in Task 1) and organizing them along consistent dimensions so the papers could be compared fairly.
I also used Elicit, a research-paper-specialized AI tool, whose independent synthesis surfaced a fourth tension - model fidelity versus deployability - that Claude's original three-tension pass had not produced. Tension 4 below is added directly from that cross-check, then re-expressed using this report's own [n] citation numbering and evidence.
Based on the cross-reference network from Task 2 and a cross-check against an independent AI synthesis (Elicit), four genuine tensions recur across the document set. Each is examined below by directly contrasting the approaches, so that Task 4 can identify which trade-offs the organization actually has to resolve.
Tension 1 - Classical OR/Metaheuristics vs. Reinforcement Learning for Scheduling
The 17-document 'Furnace & Rolling Scheduling' cluster is dominated by GA, Grey Wolf, PSO, MILP and matheuristic approaches ([2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 13, 15, 16, 19, 23, 29, 30]). A smaller but fast-growing set ([1, 11, 12, 25, 28]) replaces the optimizer with a Reinforcement Learning agent.
Synthesis: RL is not replacing OR - it is being layered on top of it. [1] and [25] both keep a classical optimization core (schedule generation, ALADIN) and use RL only for the sub-problem that is genuinely stochastic (live disturbance response, energy-media allocation under uncertainty). The dominant pattern is hybrid: OR handles the deterministic 'skeleton' schedule, RL/DRL handles real-time adaptation.
Tension 2 - Digital Twins as Passive Monitoring vs. Active Real-Time Control Substrate
Digital Twin papers ([1, 4, 10, 14, 29]) split along one axis: is the DT built to observe and predict, or to close the loop and directly drive scheduling decisions?
• Passive/predictive DT: [10] (IoT-based CSR framework) - the DT predicts rolling force and optimizes tension, but the loop closes through a human-verified control function, not autonomous rescheduling.
• Active/control DT: [29] (Digital Twin + ALTS-DT tabu search) and [1] (DT + Deep-Q-Learning) - the DT's live state directly feeds an optimizer/agent that outputs the next schedule, with under 1% simulation error ([29]) enabling this trust.
• Human-in-the-loop hybrid: [4] (I5.0 human-centric PPS) explicitly keeps a human planner validating the DT-generated plan before execution - the DT informs, a person decides.
Synthesis: the field is converging toward DTs as active control substrates ([29]'s <1% error is the enabling condition), but [4] shows that even the most DT-native architectures preserve a human validation step for the final schedule - this mirrors the process-safety argument of [9] almost exactly, even though the two clusters were built independently.
Tension 3 - Optimization Performance vs. Explainability / Human Trust
Cluster E ([9, 24, 26, 27, 31]) is not concerned with beating a benchmark - it questions whether operators will actually adopt the black-box optimizer that clusters A and B just built.
Synthesis: [9]'s LOPA-based argument generalizes the XAI cluster's message into a formal risk statement - full automation is inappropriate wherever a decision carries safety or high financial consequence, regardless of how good the underlying optimizer is.
Tension 4 - Model Fidelity vs. Deployability (added from the Elicit cross-check)
This tension was not identified in my original three-tension pass; it surfaced from Elicit's independent synthesis and is reproduced here using this report's own evidence and citation numbering. Several documents model the physical process at very different levels of detail, and higher fidelity is not free.
• Low-fidelity/fast surrogate: [2]'s GA-BP neural network predicts heat energy consumption directly from coupled production and equipment variables, at 94.7% accuracy, without simulating furnace physics - fast to run, cheap to retrain, good for screening or for training an RL agent.
• Mid-fidelity continuous dynamics: [21] rejects simple on/off/standby furnace states in favor of continuous-time dynamics embedded directly into an idle-energy function, enabling a provably optimal polynomial-time algorithm - more physically realistic, still analytically tractable.
• High-fidelity hybrid simulation: [15] combines discrete material flow with continuous energy behavior in a hybrid discrete-continuous simulation, feeding optimized plans back toward ERP/MES-level systems - the most realistic model in the set, but also the most expensive to calibrate and run.
Synthesis: fidelity and deployability trade off directly against each other, and the set as a whole implies a tiered resolution rather than a single winner - fast surrogate models ([2]-style) for screening and for training RL/DRL policies; calibrated hybrid simulation ([15]-style) for validating a candidate schedule before it reaches an operator; and hard process rules plus live measurements ([21]-style constraints) enforced at execution time regardless of which model proposed the schedule.
Bridge to Task 4
The four tensions are not independent - they resolve into a single design question: which parts of the pipeline should be optimized by OR/RL, which should run through a Digital Twin as an active control loop, which decisions require an explainable, human-verifiable interface, and which model fidelity tier is appropriate at each stage. Task 4 combines the best practices identified above, including the tiered-model resolution to Tension 4, into one integrated organizational blueprint.

Task 4 - Integrative Synthesis
Course: Managing with Artificial Intelligence - Assignment T01, Task 4
How AI was used in this task
I asked Claude to combine the four tensions from Task 3 into a single coherent system design, rather than treating them as separate recommendations, and to represent that design as a flow diagram. Claude wrote the Graphviz (dot language) code for the blueprint diagram below, defining each layer and the direction of information flow between them, then rendered it with the dot tool.
I used Elicit, a research-paper-specialized AI tool, to cross-check this blueprint against its own independently proposed six-layer architecture. Two of Elicit's concepts were missing from my original blueprint and are explicitly folded in below, with a note on where each came from: (1) an explicit receding-horizon operating loop (Observe-Predict-Optimize-Explain-Approve-Execute-Learn), and (2) a decision-priority hierarchy for resolving conflicts between safety, service, energy, stability and learning at every scheduling cycle. Elicit's recommended pilot scope (a single furnace/rolling interface on a 24-72h rolling horizon) is also adopted directly in Section 5.
Rationale: synthesis is the act of integration. Task 4 re-converges the four tensions from Task 3 into one implementable organizational blueprint, combining the best practices of DRL, Digital Twins and XAI with the metallurgical constraints (energy, tardiness, robustness, safety) established in Task 1-2, and cross-checked against an independently generated AI synthesis (Elicit).
1. The unified blueprint
2. Layer-by-layer rationale
• Digital Twin layer - the backbone, not a bolt-on. [29] shows <1% simulation error is achievable, which is the precondition for trusting a DT to drive scheduling rather than just visualize it. All other layers subscribe to this live state.
• OR/metaheuristic core stays as the deterministic skeleton. It is mature, provably optimal in several cases ([21]), and industrially proven ([30]: 1.21% energy reduction in production). Replacing it wholesale with RL is unnecessary and, per Tension 1, not what the leading papers actually do.
• RL/DRL layer is scoped narrowly to what it is good at: reacting to exogenous uncertainty (machine breakdown, spot electricity prices, demand response) that the OR core cannot re-solve fast enough for. This mirrors [1, 25]'s hybrid design exactly.
• Energy & gas-flow module is treated as a shared constraint/signal feeding both the OR core and the RL layer, not a separate silo - this reflects the orange cross-cluster bridge identified in Task 2 ([8, 9, 25, 28]).
• A model-fidelity tier sits underneath the OR core and RL layer, per Tension 4: fast surrogate models ([2]-style) for screening and RL training, calibrated hybrid simulation ([15]-style) for validating a candidate schedule, and hard process rules plus live measurements ([21]-style) enforced regardless of which model proposed the schedule.
• Explainable AI interface sits between the optimizer and the human by design, not as an afterthought - every proposed schedule or adjustment is translated into a decision-tree/counterfactual explanation ([24, 27]) before it reaches a person.
• Human planner and Safety governance layer are the final authority, directly implementing [9]'s LOPA-based conclusion: full automation is not appropriate for safety- or cost-critical decisions. The system loops back to the Digital Twin only after human/safety validation - the loop never fully closes without a person in a HiL or HoL role.
3. Operating loop (adopted from the Elicit cross-check)
Every scheduling cycle runs the same receding-horizon loop, which makes explicit how the blueprint's layers interact over time rather than just spatially:
• Observe - read current Digital Twin state (furnaces, billets/slabs, ladles, gas holders, orders, quality measurements, operator status).
• Predict - forecast near-term disturbances (order arrivals, energy prices, equipment risk) using the relevant model-fidelity tier.
• Optimize - generate a candidate schedule via the OR core, refined by the RL layer for the disturbance-response sub-problem.
• Explain - translate the candidate into a decision-tree/counterfactual explanation via the XAI interface.
• Approve - a human planner reviews and approves, adjusts, or rejects the explained recommendation.
• Execute - the approved schedule is sent to the plant; the safety governance layer retains override authority throughout.
• Learn - outcomes, overrides and rare events are logged and used to recalibrate the Digital Twin, the surrogate models and the RL reward function.
4. Decision-priority hierarchy (adopted from the Elicit cross-check)
When the blueprint's layers disagree (e.g., the RL layer proposes an energy-saving change that the feasibility check flags), the following strict priority order resolves the conflict at every cycle:
• 1. Safety and metallurgical feasibility - reject infeasible actions outright, regardless of any other benefit.
• 2. Service continuity - protect hot-material flow, due dates, and downstream bottlenecks.
• 3. Energy efficiency - minimize avoidable heating, idle energy, gas imbalance and demand peaks.
• 4. Stability - penalize unnecessary schedule churn and preserve operator confidence in the system.
• 5. Learning - retain labelled outcomes, overrides and rare events for future model improvement.
5. Where each IA mode from [9] applies
• Human on the Loop (HoL): basic process control and routine OR-generated schedules - AI acts, humans are informed and can intervene.
• Human in the Loop (HiL): RL-driven real-time rescheduling and energy-market reactions - continuous human oversight is kept because these decisions carry direct cost/robustness consequences.
• AI in the Loop (AIiL): the Explainable AI module itself - AI assists human decision-making with recommendations and explanations, but the human retains the final call, exactly as [9] prescribes for mitigation-layer-adjacent decisions.
6. Recommended pilot scope (adopted from the Elicit cross-check)
Rather than deploying the full blueprint plant-wide, start with a single reheating-furnace/rolling interface running a 24-72 hour rolling horizon. Build the Digital Twin state model and constraint library for that one interface, run the existing planner and the new OR/RL blueprint in parallel (shadow mode), and use the RL layer only to rank or propose local sequence changes - not to control the whole cell. This scope is deliberately narrow: it produces a credible value and safety case before coupling every process at once, and is developed into a concrete timeline in Task 5.
7. Net organizational value
This blueprint lets management capture the quantifiable gains documented across the set - up to 94.7% prediction accuracy ([2]), 90% tardiness reduction and 13% lower energy costs ([7]), 29.6% idle-energy savings ([16]), 1.21% integration savings ([30]) - while avoiding the adoption failure mode that Cluster E warns about: a highly optimized system that operators do not trust and therefore override or ignore. It is the logical implementable output of reconciling Tensions 1-4 from Task 3.

Executive Summary
Energy is a controllable strategic variable in steel production, not a fixed cost: reheating and heat-treatment furnaces alone can consume 60-70% of hot-rolling process energy. A structured review of 31 peer-reviewed sources on AI-based scheduling, Digital Twins and process safety - cross-checked against an independently generated AI synthesis (Elicit) - shows that double-digit energy and tardiness reductions are already demonstrated in the literature (Section 1), but only when AI is deployed as a human-governed decision-support layer, not a full replacement for operator judgment (Section 4). This report recommends a phased, staged-trust implementation (shadow mode, then advisory mode, then bounded automation only after a 90-day gate) that captures these gains while keeping safety-critical decisions in human hands.

2. Attention - The Cost of Standing Still
Every week of un-optimized scheduling is a week of avoidable cost. The gains summarized in Section 1 require no new capital equipment, only better decision-making around the equipment already installed. This is the financial case for action.
3. Interest - What Is Now Possible
• Digital Twins can now mirror the physical plant with under 1% error [29], reliable enough to drive live scheduling decisions, not just dashboards.
• Deep Reinforcement Learning and LLM-assisted RL now react to disturbances (breakdowns, spot electricity prices, demand-response events) in real time [1, 11, 25, 28], something static optimizers cannot do.
• Multi-agent and market-based coordination [18] automatically re-matches otherwise-wasted off-spec production to alternative orders.
4. Desire - Why This Is Safe to Adopt
The single most consistent finding across the safety- and trust-focused literature [9, 24, 26, 27, 31] is that full automation is the wrong target. The recommended approach is Intelligence Augmentation: AI proposes and explains, a human approves. This is not a compromise that sacrifices performance - it is what lets the organization actually capture the performance, because operators only trust and use systems whose recommendations they understand.

5. Action - Implementation Roadmap
90-Day Kickoff Gate
Before committing to the full 15-month roadmap above, run a tight 90-day kickoff to prove the approach on one cell:
• Days 0-30: establish the baseline. Select one furnace/rolling cell; document current scheduling rules, energy meters, quality limits, overrides and disturbance classes. Define success metrics before any model building starts.
• Days 31-60: build the decision substrate. Implement the asset/order/event data model, the Digital Twin state view, the hard-constraint feasibility checker, the baseline optimizer, and a schedule replay simulator.
• Days 61-90: run shadow mode. Compare the incumbent schedule with the new optimizer and RL-assisted alternatives without changing live production; review energy, tardiness, quality proxies, schedule churn, explanation usefulness and operator overrides.
• Gate decision: advance to Phase 3 (advisory mode) only if feasibility is perfect on the tested constraint set, explanations are accepted by operators, and the measured energy/service improvements survive replay and live shadow evaluation. Otherwise, fix data, constraints or reward design before expanding scope.
Bottom line: the technology to capture double-digit energy and tardiness reductions already exists and is documented across 31 independent sources. The organizational risk is not technical failure but adoption failure - a human-governed, explainable, staged rollout is what converts published research results into realized savings.
